description: Splitting code into files with require/module.exports and import/export.

screens.body:
A single 2,000-line file is a nightmare: hard to read, hard to test, scary to change. Modules fix that.

A module is just a file with a focused job — math helpers, database code, route handlers. Each file does one thing well.

You connect them by exporting values from one file and importing them into another.

options: Each file does one focused job, so code stays readable and testable
Files load faster in the browser
check.question: Why split code into modules?

code.snippet:
$ ls src
math.js   database.js   app.js   # small files, clear jobs

screens.heading: Why split code into modules?
screens.keyPoint: Modules = small files, each with one job.

screens.body:
CommonJS is Node's original module system. Two keywords do everything.

module.exports decides what leaves the file. require() pulls it into another file.

You'll see this style in tons of existing code and tutorials — it's worth recognizing even if you write the newer syntax.

options: module.exports = { add }; and const { add } = require("./math.js");
export add; and import add from math
module.exports add; and require add from math
check.question: How do you share add() from math.js using CommonJS?

screens.heading: CommonJS: require and module.exports
screens.keyPoint: module.exports sends it out. require() brings it in.

screens.body:
ESM (ECMAScript Modules) is the modern standard — the same import/export syntax browsers use.

export marks what leaves the file. import pulls it into another file. Notice the ./math.js path needs its extension.

New projects usually pick ESM. It also enables tree-shaking: bundlers can drop exported code you never import.

check.question: How do you import add() using ESM?

screens.heading: ESM: import and export
screens.keyPoint: export sends it out. import brings it in. Same idea, modern syntax.

screens.body:
Node decides which system a .js file uses by looking at package.json. The "type" field is the switch.

"type": "module" means .js files use import/export. Leave it out (or set "commonjs") and .js files use require/module.exports.

You can also be explicit per file: .mjs is always ESM, .cjs is always CommonJS, no matter what package.json says.

options: Install the esm package from npm
check.question: Your .js files should use import/export. What do you change?

screens.heading: The "type" switch

screens.body:
Modules aren't just your own files — this is also how you use installed packages.

CommonJS: const lodash = require("lodash"). ESM: import lodash from "lodash". No ./ path — Node searches node_modules for you.

Built-in modules work the same way: require("fs") or import fs from "fs". No install needed, ever.

check.question: How do you load an installed package with CommonJS?

screens.heading: Importing packages
screens.keyPoint: Bare names ("lodash") = search node_modules. No install step.

screens.body:
Named exports share several values: export function a() {} and import { a, b } from "./x.js". The names must match.

A default export shares one main thing: export default myFunction, imported as import myFunction from "./x.js" — you can name it anything.

One rule: a file gets exactly one default export. (Named exports are unlimited.)

check.question: How many default exports can a file have?

screens.heading: Named vs default exports
screens.keyPoint: Named = exact names, many allowed. Default = one, any name.

screens.body:
File paths are trickier in modules than in plain scripts. Two helpers save you.

The path module builds paths safely across operating systems: path.join("src", "app.js") uses the right slashes everywhere.

And if you ever need "the folder this file is in": CommonJS has __dirname built in; ESM uses import.meta.dirname in modern Node.

options: path.join() — it uses the correct slashes on every OS
check.question: How do you build a file path that works on Windows and Mac?

code.snippet:
const path = require("path");
console.log(path.join("src", "app.js")); // "src/app.js" on Mac/Linux

screens.heading: Paths in modules
screens.keyPoint: path.join() builds paths that work everywhere.
